A Letter from the President 


May I say how grateful I am to 
the Publisher of Canadian Camp¬ 
ing for permission to write an article 
for the magazine with news and 
information which comes across the 
President’s desk. I hope that some 
of the information will be of interest 
to those involved in camping from 
coast to coast. 

C.C.A. has taken a rather gigantic 
stride—in that our Executive is now 
a truly “National” one. As you 
know, since the Association was 
founded, the Executive moved from 
province to province every two years. 
Now there are five Vice-Presidents 
on the Executive of C.C.A. who 
represent various regions in Canada. 
I am thrilled to know that for the 
next two years, I will be working 
with Tom Creighton (Atlantic 
Provinces), Bob Lazanik, (Quebec), 
Jack Pearse (Ontario), Eileen 
Mayotte (Prairie Provinces) and 
Tanya Krisman (B.C.) I would also 
like to welcome Brian Graham of 
Toronto as the new Treasurer of 
C.C.A. and Rick Bcndera, also from 
Toronto, as the Secretary. 

The Board of C.C.A. is now made 
up of the Executive, the Provincial 
Association Presidents and the Com¬ 
mittee Chairmen. 


Many people across the country 
are still talking about the successful 
Conference recently held in Halifax 
and I wish to congratulate all of 
those who were responsible for the 
very fine organization. I would also 
like to add a personal note of thanks 
to Dave Hartry, Mrs. Betty Camp¬ 
bell, Mrs. Merrily Walker, Mrs. 
Bertie Publicover and Mrs. Marion 
Rosborough as well as Tom Creigh¬ 
ton for their efforts in making sure 
that all the delegates from other 
parts of the country were well en¬ 
tertained during their visit to Hali¬ 
fax. I was also very impressed with 
many of the new faces seen at our 
conference. In addition to learning 
more about camping, I hope that the 
delegates returned home feeling that 
they had made many new friends. 

At the conclusion of the confer¬ 
ence, certain resolutions were passed 
on to the Executive for study and 
action and I wish to comment on 
two or three points related to these 
recommendations. “The Canadian 
Camping Association hold a work¬ 
shop no later than January 31, 
1972”—a request for funds to hold 
this workshop has been submitted to 
Mr. Cor Westland, our contact man 
with the Department of Fitness and 
Amateur Sport and he has replied 


that he looks very favourably upon 
the request. It should be noted also 
that the resolution also asked that 
“all provinces have minimum stand¬ 
ards prepared so that they can be 
used in the study of provincial 
standards development and the de¬ 
velopment of national standards”. 
This request has been submitted to 
all provincial Associations. 

In the near future, all camps will 
be receiving information about the 
National Camping Day which will 
be held on Wednesday , July 21st, 
1971. Mr. Doug Dent of Victoria is 
the Chairman of this committee and 
he will be in touch with everyone 
involved in camping so that this can 
be truly a National programme. 

Kirk Wipper and his committee 
are very pleased with the response to 
the Centenary Journey Journal. 
Copies are now available through 
the C.C.A. office. Incidentally, we 
also have a few copies in the office 
of Mary Edgar’s very delightful little 
booklet “Once there was a camper”, 
which is available at $1.75. 

Finally, may I take this opportun¬ 
ity to wish each one of you a very 
happy, fun-filled, exciting, and 
successful summer. 

John Latimer

Thank You, Halifax! 


by Margaret Go van 

Seventy-five people from all across 
Canada came together for the an¬ 
nual meetings of the Canadian 
Camping Association, held in Hali¬ 
fax this year. All the provinces were 
represented except P.E.I. We missed 
them and the campers from the 
Territories. 

Halifax is a delightful place to 
have a conference. Although it is 
getting a face lift with new buildings 
there are still enough of the old to 
make you feel as if you were step¬ 
ping back into history. And the 
citadel looms over the city. And 
there's the sea, not that we saw 
much of that for we had brought 
the bad weather with us, and the 
sun did not shine on the conference. 
Some of us did manage a trip to 
Dartmouth on the ferry, and all of 
us enjoyed sea food fresh from the 
Atlantic! 

Halifax has another advantage; 
it is a small enough city for people 
to get around easily—to those eat¬ 
ing places; to hear and see Gordon 
Lightfoot; to go dancing; to attend 
the Neptune Theatre where the 
Fantastics was being played. I have 
seen it three times and this was the 
best performance of all. 

But the outstanding experience 
was that of the hospitality of the 
Nova Scotians. They did everything 
in their power to make us feel wel¬ 


come, and wanted, and that we 
mattered. Think of it! A piper in 
full regalia to pipe the head table 
contingent to their places! Nova 
Scotian pins to wear. Cars to take us 
sight seeing. People to answer our 
questions about places and things. 
And all with a smile! 

The conference started with a 
Reception and a dinner. (There had 
been a directors’ meeting before 
that.) The deputy-minister of edu¬ 
cation was there to make us all 
members of the oldest social club in 
Canada ‘L’Ordre de Bon-Temps!’ 
founded 1606. We also had a three¬ 
some singing Nova Scotian songs 
(I don’t think they were the kind 
that Dave Hartry would be teaching 
at his camps.) and they were fun. 
We found out afterwards that the 
leader who played the double bass, 
had given up a professorship at Yale 
to supervise music in Halifax public 
schools, that he also played at die 
Symphony, that he was reputed the 
best double bass player in the world! 
The annual reports from the prov¬ 
inces were interesting; even more 
interesting was to hear and see the 
representatives, and to meet them as 
friends afterwards. (New Bruns¬ 
wick was there for the first time; we 
were so pleased to have this new 
addition.) All in all it was a most 
pleasant evening, good food, fresh 
flowers, pleasant people. 


There were also two lunches. On 
Monday a speaker told anecdotes 
from Nova Scotian history. She is 
assistant librarian at the lovely Hali¬ 
fax library, and has done some 
historical writing. She told us that 
she had been asked to give us a 
resume of the history in twenty-five 
minutes, so had decided to tell of 
little, funny events instead. We all 
enjoyed her. 

At the second lunch Dave Hartry 
was the speaker, and of course had 
us all in stitches. It was his second 
luncheon address for the day, and I 
am afraid he just didn’t get anything 
to eat! 

Oh yes, we worked, I assure you. 
And under trying circumstances. 
The delegates from the western 
provinces had come in on the ‘milk 
plane’, an all-night journey with a 
stop-over at almost all the capital 
cities, with a putting on of seat belts, 
a straightening of chairs, and the 
reverse process every time. Many of 
the other planes had had to come 
down at Moncton which gave the 
delegates an extended bus trip, and 
the bus wasn’t any better than the 
ones kept for such emergencies in 
other cities. So more than half of us 
were very sleepy, and only caught 
up in time to have an equally inter¬ 
esting trip back! The results of our 
work will materialize later! 

Thank you, Halifax!

Fire-Safe 

Camping 

by Deputy Chief Bryan N. Mitchell 
Etobicoke, Ontario, Fire Department 

A wise woodsman or camper will 
say that 'one tree will make a mil¬ 
lion matches, and one match will 
destroy a million trees”. Each year 
across Canada many thousands of 
acres of forest are destroyed because 
some campers were careless with 
fire. No doubt many of these were 
novice campers who had not as yet 
learned the Fire Safety Rules, or 
others who simply disobeyed these 
rules. 

It takes nature many years to 
produce a tree but it can burn to the 
ground in a matter of minutes. 
Don't You Give Fire a Place to Start. 

SELECTING A CAMPSITE 

There are many features to look 
for in selecting and preparing a 
campsite. You are concerned about 
terrain so that you can pitch your 
tent on high ground so you won’t 
be "swamped” during a rain storm. 
You are concerned about the avail¬ 
ability of water, be it for drinking, 
swimming, fishing or boating. You 
may simply want to choose a camp¬ 
site with a view so that you can gaze 
all day across a beautiful blue lake 
or view with amazement the won¬ 
ders of a mountain range or a cas¬ 
cading waterfall. 

These are but a few of the many 
reasons for choosing a campsite. 
Others must be included that will 
ensure that you have a fire-safe 
campsite. If you intend camping in 
the trees you should select a site on 
the edge of a clearing and near 
water. Your tent will still be shaded 
from the hot sun but you will have 
a clear area for building your camp 
fire, drying your clothes and airing 
your blankets and sleeping bags. 

When selecting your tent site, try 
to keep upwind from the campfire. 
As the prevailing winds are usually 
from the west, it is advisable to camp 
on the north or west side of the 
clearing so the smoke or sparks will 
blow away from you. 


THE CAMPFIRE 

First of all, a fire permit should 
be acquired from a ranger or the 
Department of Lands and Forests. 

The campsite should be studied 
for the best place for a campfire. 
This should preferably be on a large 
fiat rock that has settled flush to the 
ground. A second choice is to scrape 
a circle at least four feet in diameter 
(preferably ten feet) in the ground 
vegetation to eliminate the danger 
of igniting the grass. Any roots of 
trees under the topsoil should be 
chopped off to prevent your camp¬ 
fire from tunnelling underground 
and starting another fire. 

A good camper must always be 
aware that his fire is not started 
under overhanging tree branches, 
particularly if they are evergreens 
such as pine, spruce, hemlock and 
cedar. 

Just as a clean house seldom 
burns, the same is true of a camp¬ 
site. While the tent is being erected 
others can be assigned the task of 
picking up loose twigs, leaves, grass 
and stones. The stones can be used 
to ring the fire circle and the twigs, 
etc., for the starting fuel. 

There are many ways of laying a 


fire. You may choose the teepee 
method, the criss-cross method (like 
building a small log cabin) or the 
trench method (a pit one foot deep 
and two or three feet long), but the 
main secret is to keep your fire small. 

In most national, provincial and 
private campgrounds this prepara¬ 
tory work has been done for you. 
You will find on your arrival that 
your campsite has been cleared of 
trees and ground vegetation. It will 
usually have a brick or stone fire¬ 
place or a welded steel grated fire 
pit. Fires should be lit in these areas 
and these areas only. Ask the park 
ranger or attendant where you may 
obtain firewood. In some parks it is 
free while others sell it in bundles 
for a nominal fee. If the firewood is 
damp it should be split with an axe 
and laid out in the sun to dry. Dry 
wood should be kept covered with a 
plastic sheet or tarpaulin to protect 
it from the rain. 

When starting a fire, use some 
newspaper, shavings, twigs, etc., 
that can be easily ignited with a 
match. NEVER USE GASOLINE, 
KEROSENE, ALCOHOL, BAR 
B-Q LIGHTER or other flammable 
liquids when lighting a fire. Each 


6 



year many careless campers are 
badly burned, disfigured and even 
lose their lives because of disobeying 
this safety rule. 

Never leave a campfire un¬ 
attended; be aware of flying sparks 
and always have pails of water 
available for rapid extinguishment. 
When retiring for the night, your 
campfire should be dampened down 
with water or smothered with dirt. 
Otherwise the ranger will haul you 
from your tent and ORDER you to 
do this. After a second reprimand 
he will order you to leave the park. 

When your stay at a campsite is 
over and it's time to pick up and 
move on, try to see that the site is 
left cleaner than it was on arrival. 
Make sure that your fire is “dead 
out”. Soak it with water until it is 
cool enough to stir with your hands. 
If no water is available then cover 
it over with damp earth to cut off 
the air supply. Remember to leave a 
supply of dry firewood for the next 
camper. He may have to set up 
camp in a rainstorm. 

COOKING AND HEATING 
EQUIPMENT 

Each year the camper is finding 
more sophisticated equipment on the 
market that is making camping that 
much easier. It wasn’t too many 
years ago that we only had a candle 
or a flashlight to see with, hot stones 
in the blankets to keep one warm at 
night and the open fire on which to 
do the cooking. But man’s technol¬ 
ogy has changed all of this. We still 
have the flashlight but we also have 
car battery-operated incandescent 
and fluorescent lights, white gaso¬ 
line (unleaded) operated lanterns 
and L.P. gas lanterns. Although the 
cooking can still be done over an 
open fire, most campers prefer the 
gasoline or L.P. gas-operated stoves 
or the charcoal barbecues or hi- 
bachis. The kerosene (coal-oil) 
wick-type heaters, the L.P. gas- 
operated catalytic tent heaters and 
the unleaded white gas (Iosol, etc.) 
tent heaters are now keeping us 
comfortable during those damp and 
chilly days and nights. 

However, these new cooking and 
heating inventions have created 
greater fire problems. They all re¬ 
quire a fuel and all of these fuels 
are flammable or, if you prefer, 
inflammable and this means that 
they will bum . 

The flammable liquids such as 
gasoline, alcohol, kerosene, should 
be stored in metal containers with a 
safety vent or spring-loaded lid. 
The MUST NOT BE STORED in 
glass bottles or plastic water jugs, 
etc. The containers should be 


painted red and be clearly marked 
to identify their contents. Smaller 
containers of manufacturers’ camp 
fuels, although not always red in 
colour, are generally well-labelled so 
we can readily identify their con¬ 
tents. All should be kept away from 
children. 

The L.P. (liquified petroleum) 
gases may be either propane or bu¬ 
tane and are purchased from the 
manufacturer in pressure-tested steel 
containers. These containers may be 
screwed directly to the stove, tent 
heater or light, thus eliminating the 
slopping of flammable liquids during 
filling, as is experienced in the other 
types of units. However, L.P. gas 
is flammable and is heavier than air. 
In the event of a leak the vapours 
will travel across the ground and 
can be easily ignited by any open 
flame. An odourant has been added 
by the manufacturer so that you can 
readily detect an L.P. gas leak. The 
smell is similar to that of a skunk or 
rotten cabbage. Should a leak be 
detected, DO NOT attempt to light 
the unit until it has been repaired. 

The naphtha, or white gasoline- 
operated, appliances also require 
that strong fire safety measures be 
enforced. One of the most important 
is good equipment maintenance. 
The principle of a gasoline stove or 
light is that the pumped up air 
pressure forces the vapourized gaso¬ 
line through a generator to the stove 
burner or the light's mantle. In order 
to keep the leather plunger operating 
properly on the air pump you must 
remember to add a few drops of oil 
periodically. Failure to do this sim¬ 
ple task may result in severe burns 
to the arms and/or face if gasoline 
vapours are forced out during pump¬ 
ing operations. 

The generators should be replaced 
as they become sluggish and mantles 
should be replaced on lanterns when 
they appear torn. Check for loose 
joints in pipe fittings and tighten 
them to prevent fuel leakage. 

The fire-safe camper makes it a 
rule to always fill his stove, light or 
heater when it is cool. Never fill 
equipment inside a tent or trailer, 
nor near an open fire. Always use a 
funnel and wipe up any excess 
spillage immediately. 

A gallon of gasoline, when com¬ 
pletely vapourized, has the explosive 
power of eighty sticks of dynamite. 
It is for this reason that we observe 
the rule of never refilling while the 
unit is hot. 

Although stoves and lights are 
manufactured under good quality 
control, they are still mechanical and 
therefore subject to failure. Inside a 


tent they have been known to ex¬ 
plode and have killed or burned the 
occupants. If at all possible we rec¬ 
ommend a flashlight or an electric 
light as the only light to use inside 
a tent. Leave the gasoline lantern 
outside the tent to illuminate your 
campsite. 

Catalytic tent heaters, whether 
gasoline or L.P. gas-operated, do not 
burn with an open flame. However, 
they still require some air to produce 
their heat by the catalytic process. 
Always remember to light these out 
of doors and then move them into 
your tent when they are operating 
smoothly. Make sure there is always 
a small amount of air entering your 
tent to replace the air used in the 
heater’s operation. Keep heaters 
away from tent fabric and bedding. 

NEVER use a gasoline or L.P. 
gas stove as a tent heater. Both these 
units burn with an open flame and 
in an air-tight tent will soon devour 
the oxygen from the air and cause 
the sleeping occupants to suffocate. 

Although most campers realize it 
is dangerous to use fuel-operated 
stoves for cooking inside a tent, they 
nevertheless continue to do this on 
those awful rainy days. How many 
of us have ever considered what 
action we would take in the event of 
a fire occurring, particularly when 
the stove is inside the tent? 

A stove fire can be extinguished 
easily if you remember the basic 
rules. Three things are required to 
have a fire— 

fuel —something that will burn; 

air —or oxygen, to keep the fire 
burning; and 

heat —or the temperature re¬ 
quired to ignite the fuel. 

These three things can be called the 
three sides of the fire triangle. In 
order to extinguish the fire you only 
have to remove one side of the 
triangle and the fire will go out. 

You can remove the fuel by turn¬ 
ing off the burner. The heat side 
can be removed by cooling it with 
water, and the air side can be re¬ 
moved by smothering it with a pan 
lid or baking soda (never salt, flour 
or baking powder) or by applying 
carbon dioxide gas from a C0 2 ex¬ 
tinguisher or treated baking soda 
from a dry chemical extinguisher. 

If the fire occurs in a frying pan 
it can be quickly smothered by slid¬ 
ing a pan lid over the pan, thus 
cutting off the air supply. You could 
also extinguish it with a C0 2 or dry 
chemical extinguisher or by sprink¬ 
ling the burning grease with baking 
soda (not salt or flour).

the YOUTH CULTURE 


and 


CAMPING 


FOREWORD 
by Don Groff 

Chairman, Publications Committee 

There exists within our present 
social structure, a sub culture usu¬ 
ally identified with the young. 
Members of this “Youth Culture’’ 
share values and life-styles which 
are different and often in conflict 
with those life-styles which are char¬ 
acteristic of older generations. Dif¬ 
ferences between these two frames 
of reference create problems for 
communication. 

Since many camp staff and camp¬ 
ers are part of the youth sub culture 
while many of our directors, spon¬ 
soring committee personnel, and 
senior staff reflect other cultural 
styles, it becomes evident that there 
is potential for breakdowns in com¬ 
munication within our camping 
family. Recognizing this, the maga¬ 
zine has solicited expressions of 
life-views from a variety of repre¬ 
sentatives of the youth culture. We 
present these for your increased 
understanding. 

The problem of communication 
became very evident within our 
Publications Committee as we re¬ 
viewed the articles and attempted to 
decide upon their suitability for 
printing, and necessity, if any, for 
editorial revision. Concerns about 
language forms and philosophies ex¬ 
pressed or implied in some of the 
articles caused sufficient apprehen¬ 
sion for some committee members 
(camp operators and directors) that 
we could not reach a consensus as 
we usually do for our editorial de¬ 
cisions. As a result, these articles 
appear by a majority but not unani¬ 
mous decision. 

Our hope is that we begin to close 
any gap which might already exist 
or be developing among the mem¬ 
bers of our camping family. 


How the Youth Culture 
Affects our Camps in 
Canada 

by Doug Caldwell 

Let us first pause and think very 
carefully before categorizing any so¬ 
cial group and endowing it with 
characteristics universal to its mem¬ 
bers. 

When we speak of a youth culture 
we are not dealing specifically with 
some sort of social movement bound 
together by a common ideology and 
set of goals. Rather we must recog¬ 
nize a set of people as diversified in 
their beliefs as any other given age 
group in our society. 

The very phrase ‘youth culture’ 
all too often conjures up visions of a 
long-haired, drug-oriented, morally 
deficient, radical counter-culture. It 
is my hope that we can collectively 
endeavour to reject this fallacious 
generalization and in its place sub¬ 
stitute youth interpretations with a 
little more relevance and bearing to 
reality. Youth is not an entity to be 
feared and suppressed; rather they 
are human beings, products of them¬ 
selves and generations before them. 
They are the rational continuation 
in the progress of mankind and 
should be interacted with as such, 
not to be scorned but to be com¬ 
municated with and encouraged in 
our search for a better world. 

Although acknowledging that 
there is no typical or average youth, 
I still find it logical to make use of a 
few generalizations that may very 
well apply to a majority of today’s 
youth. 

I see in the young a reason for 
optimism. Perhaps it would be easier 
for governments if they did not have 


to cope with the varying concepts 
and ideals of the youth culture. We 
could then be dealing with a seem¬ 
ingly more harmonious culture . . . 
no more demonstrations, riots, and 
confrontations. But in this hypo¬ 
thetical situation I can only visualize 
the deeper tragedy of moral apathy. 
There are conditions in our society 
that are undesirable and if we are to 
avert die ugliness of future confron¬ 
tations we must be willing to listen 
understandingly and act upon rea¬ 
sonable suggestions. We can not 
afford to suppress the ideas that may 
be the raw materials for a brighter 
future. By this I am not saying that 
we must condone all of their beliefs, 
but if communication is our goal, 
then we must be prepared to listen 
sympathetically and leave the chan¬ 
nels open, for if diey are closed, 
frustration will result and out of this 
will emerge alienated youth, lacking 
trust and respect towards an older 
generation. 

Our Canadian camps are involved 
with over four-hundred thousand 
campers every summer. We are, 
needless to say, in a position of sig¬ 
nificant influence whereby we have 
an obligation far beyond that of 
supplying children with ‘a happy 
summer in the healthy outdoors’. We 
are dealing now with the adults of 
the future. We must strive to set 
high moral standards and yet we 
often seem to be confused as to 
whether this youth culture is in fact 
an example of positive morality. 

Is there any moral significance in 
a male staff member with long hair? 
Should we be discriminatory towards 
staff members who have used drugs? 
How far should we go towards hir¬ 
ing staff members who do not have 
ideas in keeping with the philoso¬ 
phies of the established order? These 
are problems we must face when 
confronted with the emergence of 
the new youth culture. The directors 
and staff of each individual camp 
have the responsibility of the final 
decision in answering these ques¬ 
tions. 

While it is not my purpose to pass 
value-judgement on these problems, 
it is evident to me that we must not 
reject new life-styles on the basis 
that they are not in keeping with 
those of ours and therefore must be 
wrong. It is important that we put 
aside our personal bias and take a 
long and objective look at their sig¬ 
nificance in a world that is rapidly 
changing.

The Youth Culture and 
Camping 

by Bob Osborne, 

Trent University 


Camps play a very active role in 
society today. A successful camp 
serves the needs of its members. As 
the needs of the participating mem¬ 
bers change so must the camps. The 
purpose of a camp is not only to 
provide a vacation for its members 
during the summer months but also 
to instill in them a sense of well 
being; “Mens sana in corpore sano”. 

The youth of our society are, for 
the most part, a camps most active 
members and therefore it is impor¬ 
tant to be aware of die changes that 
are affecting youth today. The ad¬ 
vent of the 70s saw with it, what 
is sometimes referred to as the emer¬ 
gence of a “youdi culture”. Many of 
today’s youth are dissatisfied with 
the existing structures present in so¬ 
ciety and are attempting to effect a 
change that will make their lives 
more meaningful. As a result there 
has been the emergence of the 
“youth culture”. A new system of 
values has been equated with, and a 
sound basis for an underlying phil¬ 
osophy has been built upon, an in¬ 
creasing insistence for naturalism. 
This type of philosophy is by no 
means new to one who has studied 
Thoreau. The youth of today how¬ 
ever are aware of the pressing ur¬ 
gency of their task while ecologists 
predict the complete breakdown of 
life by the year 2000. 

The frantic pace of technological 
advancement and the resulting ten¬ 
sions are totally alien to the con¬ 
sciousness of the individual at sum¬ 
mer camp. At camp the focus is on 
survival in a natural environment 
through harmony with nature. What 
better place than camp to plant and 
nourish the idea of naturalism? 
Rocky shores, sparkling blue waters, 
whispering pines, sunlight dancing 
on the forest floor, the scamper of 
squirrels, the glowing embers of an 
all night watch—these all are too 
soon gone unless die voice of youth 
is heeded. 

What means are best used to 
convey this philosophy? 

An unstructured program which 
is stimulated by “whim” or rather a 
sense of well-being in body and 
mind is probably the ideal method. 
This places a great responsibility on

Youth Culture X Camping 

by ed la Pierre 

(Ed is currently a student at Dal - 
housie University, Halifax. He has 
served as Counsellor in Training 
Director at Y.M.C.A. Big Cove 
Camp, Nova Scotia.) 

(This article is unedited.') 


The contents of this article are 
directed to all camp directors, ad¬ 
ministrators and leaders who are 
interested and concerned in trying to 
help bridge the gap that exists be¬ 
tween our Canadian youth and 
themselves in camping. The gap is 
present and is widening. There are 
many factors which account for its 
growth and development. It is a 
result of change in values, attitudes 
and ideals. 

Why do teenagers turn off to the 
camping experience they enjoyed as 
nine and eleven year olds? Why do 
they look upon going to camp as a 
drag, a put off? A simple answer 
would be that their needs are no 
longer being satisfied through such 
experiences and they seek other 
avenues in which they feel more 
alive and comfortable. 

To understand why camping is a 
drag we have to analyze the com¬ 
ponents of our youth culture and 
then stand back and look at the 
present Canadian Camping scene. 
The mobility of teenagers is their 
chief driving force. They are per¬ 
petually involved in multi-dimen¬ 
sional experiences. Most are inter¬ 
acting with drugs, sex and/or music. 

Moving about from Vancouver to 
Halifax with very limited funds and 
a desire to be relaxed, free and not 
be hasseled by authority is a happen¬ 
ing which more and more youth are 
doing and will continue to do in 
greater numbers. Scenes like the 
Strawberry Festival in Mosport, Ont. 
and Joan Baez in Waleville, N.S. 
served as a coming together; immer¬ 
sion in individual experiences which 
bring personal satisfaction through 
sensuous contact; experiences which 
have very loose ground rules and 
which leave room for the individ¬ 
ual’s likes and dislikes. 

For some the whole of Canada 
becomes a camping ground. Finding 
it wherever they can, moving from 
one town to another, in and out of 
cities, meeting and leaving people 
who are also on the road; crashing at 
a friend’s place, a youth hostel, a 


field; satisfying natural biological 
needs and not necessarily looking 
for companionship or security. Time 
becomes suspended as the past, 
present and future and it becomes 
endless infinity. These experiences 
are quite different from die usual 
camping trip. 

Camping means to most campers 
—going to one specific place for a 
definite amount of time. Being lim¬ 
ited to certain boundaries. Having in 
most cases a definite time table 
which means getting up at sunrise 
to best enjoy whatever it is you have 
or should enjoy. Eating at a set time, 
specially prepared menues. Most 
Canadian camps are unisexual. Most 
camp administrators and supervisors 
look upon their authority as replac¬ 
ing that of the parent. Sex is worried 
about and it is hoped that no acci¬ 
dent happens which would put 
Camp Director Short Pants in die 
embarrassing situation of relaying 
the news to dear modier. Control is 
assured by authority rather dian 
individual responsibility. Most camp 
directors and senior staff are fla¬ 
grantly ignorant about drugs. They 
know only the negative side of the 
drug culture. Sunday services re¬ 
place church going where the camp 
director feels very secure in per¬ 
forming these special functions be¬ 
cause this is what he can best do. 

Let’s put a few things together. If 
camps are to become a happening for 
teenagers they must be informal in 
structure and operation. Resident 
camps should be controlled by the 
campers themselves. They should 
become a commune. Leaders who 
are in tunc with what’s real and 
happening should be sharing the 
experience with them. University 
students with specialized skills who 
can communicate should be hired as 
leaders and be paid adequate sal¬ 
aries. Directors; with a sensitive 
open approach to people and their 
problems, an M.A. in one or more 
related fields such as psychology, 
sociology, recreation teaching, phys¬ 
ical education, varied experiences on 
the road, should be appointed for a 
period of two years at which time 
their performance would be eval¬ 
uated by: (a) the campers (b) Staff 
(c) Supervisors. Camps which are 
close to major towns and cities could 
become meeting places for Canadian 
youths who are on the move. These 
camps should become year round 
hostels supported by fees and pro¬ 
vincial and/or federal subsidies. 

It’s partly up to you. Camping 
could become a happening for many 
Canadian youths.

Tennis May Be Dear, 
Sphairee Is Not 

by Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D., 

Director, Camp Ponacka 


A few years ago the Canadian 
General Electric Company suddenly 
transferred one of its engineers to 
Australia. John Lucas, his wife and 
six children, spent two years “down 
under” and then returned to their 
one-hundred-year old farmhouse on 
the outskirts of Peterborough. Soon 
after they returned they invited us 
for a game of Sphairee, which, of 
course, left us somewhat baffled. 
Upon enquiry we found out that a 
new type of tennis game had been 
invented and that its name was 
Sphairee (Sfy-Ree) — from the 
Greek word for ball, “Sphaira”. 
Since their Sphairee court was built 
next to their tennis court, a good 
comparison could be made of the 
two games. It soon became evident 
that children are much keener on 
the smaller game than on regular 
tennis. The reason is not hard to 
find. A rank beginner can easily 
learn to handle the small racquet 
and instead of missing eight balls 
out of ten, he probably has that ratio 
of successful hits. On the smaller 
court one is not chasing balls half of 
one’s playing time because the 
Sphairee ball is perforated like a 
practice golf ball and hence its flight 
is quickly brought to an end. 

Frederick Beck of Sydney Uni¬ 
versity, developed the game in order 
to enable young Australians to de¬ 
velop tennis skills, even if a tennis 


court is unavailable. Sphairee can 
be played on an average size drive¬ 
way and it becomes the rallying 
point of the neighbourhood, and a 
place for family fun. Mr. Beck also 
found that a great many aging tennis 
players could no longer stand the 
strain of a regular game but found 
the new game challenging enough 
to maintain agility and general fit¬ 
ness. 

At our camp we installed two 
adjacent courts by cementing the 
required area. The courts are always 
in great demand and we are plan¬ 
ning to build a third court this 
summer. The equipment is inexpen¬ 
sive to buy, the courts require no 
upkeep, and the initial investment is 
not large as no fencing is required. 
Since the game was invented ten 
years ago, it has spread all through 
Australia and even into the United 
States, where it is gaining favour on 
playgrounds and in schools. 
EQUIPMENT : 

Bats shall be constructed of five-ply 
wood, W' thick, plus or minus 
1/32", faced with cork or shallow 
pimple rubber sheeting. The bat 
shall be no more than 15" long and 
7 Vi" wide (overall), with the mini¬ 
mum width of the bat maintained 
for at least 5" of the length. Handles 
may be made of any material and 
may be wrapped according to the 
player’s desires. 


Balls shall be constructed of per¬ 
forated heavy gauge plastic mea¬ 
suring 2Vi" in diameter. (In Can¬ 
ada, balls similar to these can be 
purchased in most sporting goods 
stores under the name, “Fun ball”. 
They are somewhat heavier than 
they should be but they will do). 

Net — The net shall be approx¬ 
imately 18" high and ten or more 
feet long, tight enough to keep the 
ball from going through. 

Court — The court shall be 20' 
long and 9' wide, with safety clear¬ 
ances on all sides. All lines shall be 
1"- lYi" wide, white or yellow in 
color. Any hard surface of concrete 
or asphalt is generally suitable. The 
net shall be tautly stretched over the 
middle of the court, 10' from either 
end, with the top edge measuring 
2 3 Vi" - 24" above the court surface 
at center court. 

GENERAL RULES: 

The game is played like tennis, 
with three major exceptions: 

(1) The server is permitted only 
one serve, unless the ball 
touches the net. 

(2) Serves must be delivered un¬ 
derhand, from below the level 
of die hips. 

(3) In singles: the server must 
allow the return of the ball to 
bounce, but thereafter need 
not do so. 

In doubles: both the server’s and 
the receiver’s partners must stand 
behind the base line until the serve 
is struck. 

RULES OF PLAY 

(1) Contestants “play for the 
serve”, before a set commences, 
by first playing a special rally 
in which the ball is batted over 
die net diree or more times. 
The winner serves in the first 
game and thereafter the serve 
is alternated between oppon¬ 
ents. Ends are changed after 
the first game and thereafter 
whenever the games total of 
both players is an uneven 
number. 

(2) The serve is delivered from 
behind the base line, to one 
side of center, with the first 
game serve delivered from be¬ 
hind the server’s right side of 
the base line. After each point, 
the serving side is alternated. 
In every case, the server must 
serve to the diagonally opposite 
box. 

(3) A point is scored when one 
player fails to return the ball 
within the court. A ball which 
lands on any line is “in”. If a 
player returns (volleys) a ball 
which would otherwise be 


10 

















1 :' 


—_ 20 ft _J 

C 

) 



W 

z 





9 ft 


SPHAIREE COURT LAYOUT 


‘out”, the ball is still regarded 
in play. If a player catches a 
ball before it bounces out, or 
if it touches any part of his 
clothing or body (other than 
the thumb and fingers holding 
the bat), a point is scored 
against him. 

(4) The point score is identical to 
that of tennis; 15, 30, 40 and 
Game. At 40-All (tie) the 
score is called “deuce”. When 
deuce is called, the next point 
is “advantage” to the player 
scoring it. If he scores the sub¬ 
sequent point after scoring the 
advantage, he wins the game. 
If he loses the next point after 
holding the advantage, the 
score reverts to deuce until one 
player scores two consecutive 
points and wins the game. 

(5) A “set” normally ends when 
one player reaches a score of 
six games. In championship 
play, advantage sets are played; 
a player cannot claim a set 
until he has scored six or more 
games AND he has established 
a lead of two clear games. A 
“rubber” normally consists of 
the best of three advantage sets 
but the number of games in a 


set and the number of sets in 
a rubber may be varied if fixed 
in advance. 

(6) In doubles, the rules are es¬ 
sentially the same, with the 
exceptions noted in the Gen¬ 
eral Rules and the require¬ 
ment that the serve must be 
rotated between players on a 
side. 


EQUIPMENT IS AVAILABLE 
FROM: 

Mrs. Kay Lucas, 

RR #4, Peterborough, Ont. 

To equip one court with four 
bats, three balls and a net, will 
probably cost less than $15.00. 

If you decide to introduce the 
game, I know you will not regret it.

Dc par la nature meme du Camp 
de Jour, les enfants, ne couchant pas 
au camp doivent etre vehicules 
matin et soir. 

Les moyens de transport utilises 
presentcment dans les camps de jour 
sont l’autobus, le mini-bus, le sta¬ 
tion-wagon et l’automobile. Plus tard 
devrons-nous peut-etre ajouter l’he- 
licoptere, avion etc. 

Pour les camps peu nombreux 
c’est ordinairement le personnel du 
camp qui transporte les enfants 
chaque jour dans leur propre auto 
moyennant ajustement de salaire. 
Des parents, pour diminuer le cout 
de leur enfant acceptent aussi de 
transporter d’autres enfants. 

Pour les camps d’oeuvres plus 
considerables on designe des points 
de rassemblement (en face d’eglise, 
decole) pour les departs et les 
retours par groupes. 

Cette partie importante de l’or- 
ganisation dun camp de jour doit 
etre une des preoccupations pre¬ 
mieres du directeur. 

Quel moyen de transport utili- 
sera-t-il? 

1— S’il utilise les autos du person¬ 
nel cela implique que le per¬ 
sonnel 

a) est age d’au moin 21 ans 

b) qu’il ne demeure pas au 
camp (a moins que le camp 
soit tres pres de la ville) et 
de ce fait revaluation et le 
reajustement de la program- 
mation sont rendus diffi- 
ciles. 

2— Si le camp est proprietaire d’au- 
tobus, le cout d’operation est 
trop eleve, permis, assurances, 
reparations, depreciations, per¬ 
sonnel, specialise: chauffeurs, 
mecaniciens, a moins que les 
autobus ne servent 12 mois . . . 
et encore. 

PLANIFICATION 
Comment choisir la compagnie 
d!autobus? 

Proceder par soumission. Ne pas

SON TRANSPORT 


Huguette L. Dagenais 
Camp de Jour Les Greves 


necessairement arreter son choix sur 
le cout le plus bas, mais sur les 
garanties que les exigences du camp 
seront respectees. 

Que doit'on incline dans la demande 
de soumission? 

1— Le nombre d’autobus requis. 
S’informer du nombre d'enfants 
que legalement un autobus peut 
contenir suivant sa grandeur, et 
d’apres le nombre d’enfants 
attendus au camp, faire le 
compte. 

2— Fixer les dates et les heures pre¬ 
cises des departs et des retours. 

3— Fournir un trajet preliminaire 
pour faciliter un calcul approxi¬ 
mate de la distance. 

4— S’assurer que tous les autobus 
soient porteurs de permis com- 
merciaux. (Verifier les lois pro- 
vinciales a ce sujet.) 

5— Exiger une copie des assurances 
couvrant chaque autobus. 

6— Preciser si les chauffeurs restent 
ou non au camp durant le jour. 

Lorsque la compagnie est choisie, 
il faudra avant de signer le contrat: 

1— Que la compagnie obtienne le 
permis de la Regie des Trans¬ 
ports. 

2— Que le directeur verifie si les 
polices d’assurances, le permis, 
et le No. de serie correspondent 
au meme autobus. 

Cela semble superflu mais il arrive 
que les compagnies peu conscien- 
cieuse transportent les licences et les 
assurances d’un autobus a l’autre. 

Pour assurer une plus grande pro¬ 
tection, il est suggere que le camp 
prenne une assurance responsabilite 
additionnelle de “non-proprietaire”. 
Toute cette operation doit se faire 
au moins 4 mois avant l’ouverture 
du camp. 

ORGANISATION 
Aidant le camp: 

Des trajets clairs et detailles in¬ 
diquant les points de rassemblement 
avec noms de rues et sens unique 


doivent etre prepares ainsi qu’une 
liste des enfants a prendre a chaque 
point de rassemblement. 

Pendant le camp: 

La direction du camp doit: 

1 — Assurer la presence d’un moni- 
teur pour accompagner les en¬ 
fants, laissant au chauffeur 
toute l’attention necessaire pour 
conduire. 

2— Donner le nom d’une personne, 
a qui le directeur delegue son 
autorite pour tout ce qui con- 
cerne le transport, et le No. de 
telephone du camp afin que les 
chauffeurs sachent qui rejoindre 
en cas de retard cause par une 
defectuosite mecanique, une 
crevaison, etc. 

3— Fournir une liste des reglements 
du camp concernant les chauf¬ 
feurs. 

4— Fournir s’il y a lieu, un endroit 
pour le lavage quotidien des 
autobus. 

La compagnie doit: 

1— Fournir une liste de ses chauf¬ 
feurs avec leur destination. 

2— Afficher les reglements de la 
compagnie dans chaque auto¬ 
bus. 

3— Dans chaque autobus il doit y 
avoir une trousse de secours 
complete. 

4— Fournir des sacs plastifies au cas 
ou les enfants seraient malades. 

5— Fournir des autobus propres et 
en bonne conditions. 

6— Si il y a plusieurs autobus, un 
des chauffeurs doit etre mecani- 
cien, pour effectuer les repara¬ 
tions mineures en cours de 
route. 

7— Fournir le nom d’une personne 
responsable, avec qui le camp 
fera toujours affaires. 

8— Employer des chauffeurs re- 
sponsablcs et qui aiment et 
respectent les enfants. 

Le succes d’un camp de jour 
repose en grande partie sur son 
transport. Voyons-y sagement. 




THE DAY CAMP AND 
TRANSPORTATION 

Huguette L. Dagenais 
Day Camp “Les Greves” 

At a day camp, the children who 
are not sleeping at the camp must 
be transported morning and night. 

The transportation used presently 
in day camps are the bus, mini-bus, 
station-wagon and car. Later on we 
may be adding the helicopter, air¬ 
plane, etc. 

In camps where there are a small 
number of children, usually the staff 
transport the children every day 
using their own car, having in return 
a compensation on their salary. In 
order for the parent to cut the cost 
of their children’s stay at camp, they 
will agree to transport other chil¬ 
dren. 

For the camps where there are a 
large number of children, a meeting 
point is designated, say in front of 
the church or school, for departures 
and returns in groups. This impor¬ 
tant part of a day camp organization 
must be one of the first concerns of 
the Director. 

What type of transportation will 
he use? 

1) If he uses the staffs cars, it will 
be necessary that the staff: 

a) be 21 years old; 

b) must not live at the camp 
(unless the camp is situated 
near the town) which 
makes it difficult for the 
evaluation and re-adjusting 
of the programming. 

2) If the camp owns a bus, the cost 
of operation is too high, permit, 
insurance, repairs, depreciation, 
specialized staff: drivers, mech¬ 
anics; unless the bus is used for 
12 months . . . and even more. 

PLANNING 

How to choose a bus company ? 

Do it by tender. Do not neces¬ 
sarily choose the company that has 
the lowest bid, but rather consider 
the camp requirements and ensure 
that they will be respected. 

What should you include in the 
request for tenders? 

1) The number of buses required. 
Enquire how many children a 
bus is legally authorized to 
transport according to its size, 
and after calculating the num¬ 
ber of children who will be com¬ 
ing to the camp, see how many 
buses you need. 

2) Give the exact dates and hours 
of departures and returns. 

3) Give a preliminary itinerary to 
facilitate the calculation of 
distance. 


4) Ensure that all buses have a 
commercial permit. (Verify the 
provincial laws to this effect) 

5) Request a copy of the Insurance 
Policy covering each bus. 

6) Establish if the drivers will stay 
or not at the camp during the 
day. 

When the company has been 
chosen but before signing the con¬ 
tract, the following should be done: 

1) The company should obtain a 
permit from the Transport De¬ 
partment. 

2) The director should verify if the 
insurance policies, the permit 
and the serial number corres¬ 
pond to the same bus. 

This may seem to be unnecessary 
but sometimes a company will trans¬ 
fer licenses and insurances from one 
bus to another. 

In order to have better protection, 
it is suggested that the camp takes 
an additional liability insurance of 
“non-owner”. This should be done 
at least 4 months before the opening 
of the camp. 

ORGANIZATION 
Before the camp : 

Detailed and clear routes showing 
the meeting points with street names 
should be prepared as well as a list 
of children to be picked up at each 
meeting point. 

During the camp : 

The camp management must: 

1) Ensure that a monitor is present 
to escort the children, leaving 
the driver without the responsi¬ 
bility of the children while 
driving. 


2) Give the name of a person to 
whom the Director grants his 
authority for everything that 
concerns transportation, and the 
telephone number of the camp 
in order for the drivers to know 
whom to contact in case of a 
delay due to mechanical diffi¬ 
culties, flat, etc. . . . 

3) Give a list of the camp regula¬ 
tions regarding the drivers. 

4) Provide, if necessary, a location 
for the daily washing of the bus. 

The company must : 

1) Give a list of its drivers with 
their destination. 

2) Post the company regulations in 
each bus. 

3) Have in each bus a first aid kit. 

4) Provide some plastic bags in the 
bus in case children become 
sick. 

5) Provide clean buses and in good 
condition. 

6) If there are many buses, one of 
the drivers must be a mechanic 
in order to make minor repairs 
during the trip. 

7) Give the name of a responsible 
person with whom the camp 
will always deal. 

8) Employ responsible drivers who 
like and respect children. 

The success of a day camp lies in 

its transportation. See to it wisely. 

Translated by 
Translation Department, 
Administration Centre 
for Sports and 
Recreation, Ottawa

HOMESICKNESS 

DIAGNOSIS and PREVENTIVE MEASURES 


by M. C. MacCulloch, Director 

Bolton Summer Camp; — Rotary 
Unit 


Often in the development of the 
child there has been little or no 
emphasis placed upon living away 
from home. The parents, for a 
variety of reasons, have provided 
the child with a sense of security 
that is more detrimental than ad¬ 
vantageous when he finally is forced 
to leave the nest. 

Most summer camps can count 
on their share of homesickness, es¬ 
pecially among the younger camp¬ 
ers. Very often, older campers, 
ashamed of their feelings, will dis¬ 
guise homesickness and present 
their counsellor with what appears 
to be a distinctly different behav¬ 
ioural problem. The tears are miss¬ 
ing but the symptoms are there and 
the treatment remains the same for 
all age levels. 

How Do You Diagnose Homesick¬ 
ness? 

By close and careful observation, 
the counsellor can constantly be on 
the lookout for the concerns and 
needs of his campers. The home¬ 
sick camper can sometimes be 
spotted as he comes off the bus. 
Other times, it does not make itself 
evident until the excitement of 
opening day has ebbed away and 
the camper is faced with the end¬ 
less weeks until he goes home. 

Usually the child wears his prob¬ 
lem on his sleeve. He is constantly 
moping and obviously depressed 
and spiritless in spite of the most 
energetic and ambitious programme 
planned by the camp staff. The 
gloominess which prevails often de¬ 
velops into whimpering and even 
uncontrollable crying, depending 
upon the degree of homesickness. 
Sometimes the camper is not so eas¬ 
ily spotted. Instead of outward re¬ 
actions, he withdraws from the 


group, sits alone, and does not get 
the attention of the staff which he 
deserves, by virtue of his being such 
a “quiet” camper. 

With the older, more mature 
camper, homesickness is very often 
diagnosed by asking the camper 
what is bothering him. If the case 
is a severe one, and the camper has 
any kind of a relationship with 
someone on the staff, he will tell 
the counsellor that he wants to go 
home. Sometimes with the adoles¬ 
cent, whose self-esteem is not at its 
peak, the answers are not so evi¬ 
dent. 


What Causes Homesickness in 
Campers? 

The following list is by no means 
exhaustive. It is merely included to 
provide the novice counsellor with 
some of the factors which might 
cause homesickness in his campers. 
1. First time away from mother, 
sibling, environment. 

Does not feel familiar with his 
new environment, often so di¬ 
ametrically opposed to his “city 
life”. 

Too strong an attachment be¬ 
tween the camper and the ab¬ 
sentee parent, friend, or even 
pet. 

Sent to camp against his will. 
Misses his daily activities and 
play areas of the city. 

Camp programme offers little 
with which he is familiar, so, 
therefore, he is uninterested in 
that which is new; hence, bore¬ 
dom. 

Lacking basic camp skills and 
interest in the more “primitive” 
aspects of camp life. 

No one on staff has shown any 
real concern for him; due to 


2 . 


3. 


4. 

5. 


7. 


8 . 


numbers and opening day pro¬ 
gramming, counsellor has given 
very little personal attention. 

9. Over-protective “mothers” have 
over-exhibited their anxieties; 
overprotection or overdomi¬ 
nance have left the child with 
little self-confidence. 

10. Timidity — fear of “bullies”, 
ridicule, fear of water or of the 
dark. 

11. Lack of privacy in the camp 
cabins. 

12. Physical factors — such as bed¬ 
wetting, constipation. 

13. Inadequate spending money, 
or personal effects in compar¬ 
ison with more fortunate camp¬ 
ers. 

14. Physical handicaps or peculiar¬ 
ities, such as stammering, 
limping, cross-eyes. 

What Can the Counsellor Do as 
Preventive Measures Against Home¬ 
sickness? 

The fundamental rule of thumb 
is to be gentle. Homesickness is a 
very delicate problem and like all 
personal problems should be treated 
wisely, cautiously, and with kid- 
gloves. To ridicule, or point out the 
“silliness” of the situation is to 
waste one’s energy. By the same 
token, the “slap on the back” ap¬ 
proach is of no value. A homesick 
camper can not control his reactions 
and a word will not provide a cure 
for him. Rather through careful 
planning before the campers arrival, 
and by the proper attitude, the coun¬ 
sellor can aid immeasurably in the 
camper’s personal growth, the ef¬ 
fects of which will be measured 
long beyond the camper’s brief sum¬ 
mer holiday at camp.

To give a human being dignity is 
one of the far-reaching effects a 
good counsellor can have on his 
campers. 

1. The counsellor should prepare 
for his campers. The cabin 
name should be evident, it 
should be decorated, and camp¬ 
er names on the bunks as well 
as on the lockers, immediately 
lets the camper know that he 
belongs. 

2. Sometimes in smaller camps, 
the staff can meet with the 
campers before they come to 
camp. In other cases, where 
the numbers are small, a per¬ 
sonal letter from the counsellor 
will establish an enviable rap¬ 
port with the campers. 

3. The counsellor must know the 
names of his campers. This 
means, from the administrative 
level, the camper lists must be 
drawn up in advance, but the 
result is worth the labour. For 
a counsellor to know the names, 
and perhaps background of 
his campers immediately puts 
them at ease. Nothing makes 
you feel more insignificant 
than to watch your leader 
grope for your name on a list. 
(A lesson for senior staff on 
the night of pre-camp training, 
might be obvious here also. 
Counsellors can feel lost on 
that first night in camp also.) 

4. Senior staff should prepare for 
opening day also. A welcoming 
committee to meet the cars and 
buses, will welcome old camp¬ 
ers back again and make new 
campers feel that they are in 
experienced hands. The staff 
should watch for the usual 
stragglers who arrive early or 
late. They particularly need to 
see the welcome mat. Enthusi¬ 
asm should run like water. 
Welcoming signs, such as 
“Welcome” or “Yeah, Mohawk 
Section” are good for younger 
boys. Surely the first camp day 
is at least as important and sig¬ 
nificant as the last. Cabin 
name cards above the dining 
room tables get everyone orien¬ 
tated. Perhaps even name tags 
for the cabin group are in or¬ 
der. Nicknames should always 
be respected. If the camper 
prefers “Skip” there is no rea¬ 
son to call him “Wardell” just 
because vour list says so. In 
short, KNOW YOUR CAMP¬ 
ERS. 

5. Check with the Section Head 
concerning the case history of 


your campers in advance of 
their arrival. Watch the camp¬ 
ers subject to constipation, 
diarrhea, overactivity, hay fe¬ 
ver, allergies, etc. Illnesses can 
often breed homesickness. 

6. A very close contact with the 
campers on those first few days 
will later provide you with 
much more freedom and less 
worry later on. Once the cabin 
learns the routines and be¬ 
comes a unit, most of the per¬ 
sonal behavioural problems will 
disappear. Homesick campers 
should be carefully supervised 
during rest hours and evening 
hours as well as on Sunday 
when the programme is rela¬ 
tively free with plenty of open 
periods. 

7. Activities and programmes that 
appeal to the homesick camper 
can be stressed. The homesick 
boy, of course, should be en¬ 
couraged to participate to the 
fullest. A busy camper, doing 
what he enjoys, will sometimes 
solve your problem. 

8. The Section Director or Head 
Counsellor should be notified 
at the earliest opportunity. He 
not only can offer suggestions 
but sometimes can keep his eye 
on your problem or even take 
the camper “under his wing”. 

9. In open periods of time, the 
camper should be encouraged 
in his hobbies and he should be 
permitted to do what he enjoys 
the most about camping. This 
will let the camper know that 
the counsellor really thinks of 
him and respects him as an in¬ 
dividual. 

10. The necessary rules and regu¬ 
lations of the camp should be 
gone over in detail, as well as 
the daily schedule of activities 
so that security will be built 
up between the camper, his 
counsellor and his environ¬ 
ment. New duties should be 
broken into gradually so that 
the camper is not overwhelmed 
by this new way of doing 
things, and in this way, camp¬ 
ing skills which may be lack¬ 
ing, may be developed, Proced¬ 
ure in dining room, operation 
of the camp library, interest 
groups, swimming programme, 
care of property, medical pro¬ 
cedures, etc. will soon become 
familiar to the camper if pa¬ 
tience and understanding arc 
exercised. 

11. From the very beginning, 
the opening day programmes 


should involve the entire cab¬ 
in of campers. This gives them 
a sense of group unity, and of 
belonging without the need to 
stand out as an individual — 
at least on opening day. Short 
hikes together, an outdoor 
game where all can participate, 
a scavenger hunt, or a comic 
hunt in the evening, followed 
by a campfire with the whole 
section attending, will get the 
campers, the counsellors, and 
the section, off on the right 
foot. A happy first day will give 
the campers the feel of the 
camp quicker than anything 
that can be said by the leaders. 

12. On the second day, each boy 
should be talked with by the 
counsellor, concerning what he 
would like to do at camp. The 
counsellor’s job then becomes, 
by guidance and purposeful 
planning, to direct the child 
into programmes and activit¬ 
ies where he will achieve as 
many of his personal goals as is 
possible. 

If homesickness persists and the 
counsellor cannot find remedies for 
it, it becomes the responsibility of 
the Section Head. If the counsellor 
cannot cope with the problem with¬ 
out sacrificing the well-being of the 
rest of his cabin, the camper should 
first be given individual attention 
by perhaps transferring him to a 
cabin where he has friends, or 
brothers. If hysterical behaviour de¬ 
velops, as long the the leader’s san¬ 
ity is intact, it should be ignored. 
Hysteria must have an audience. It 
is a method of gaining some end, 
such as attention or one’s own way. 
Very often, if played to tiredness, 
the child will cease, seeing that his 
actions are ineffective. These cases 
are rare indeed and so serious is 
such a child’s problem that no camp 
in twelve days can expect to solve 
the condition. The parents then 
should be notified by the Director 
and the child should return home. 
Perhaps a year or two will make all 
the difference and this particular 
aspect of the child’s behavioural 
growth will have matured. 

In any case, the key note is un¬ 
derstanding. All of the staff should 
go out of their way to help the child 
come to terms with his fear so that 
he may develop as a human being. 
To send the camper home the first 
day is to cheat him. Every oppor¬ 
tunity and means that the Director 
deems necessary shoidd be given to 
the camper to conquer “fear itself\

Visitors at Camp? 


Most of the following camp 
policies favor visiting by par¬ 
ents. Let us hear from camps 
that have a “No Visitors’' 
policy. —Editor 


CAMP PONACKA 

We encourage parents to visit 
their sons for some very obvious 
reasons. The child spends eleven 
months with his parents and he is 
bound to talk about camp a great 
deal. Since camp forms a very im¬ 
portant part of his young life, par¬ 
ents, grandparents, brothers and 
sisters should share in this aspect of 
his experience. It gives the parents 
a chance to assess the camp, to meet 


the counsellor and Director. It gives 
the child a chance to show his fam¬ 
ily what seems most important to 
him. 

If it were possible, every day 
should be visitors’ day. This would 
spread visiting over a large period of 
time and few outside people would 
be at camp at one time. In this way 
the camp would run normally and 
this is what parents should witness. 

As the Director, I like to have the 
opportunity of talking to each parent 
and if visitors’ day is every day, it is 
difficult for me to plan my own time. 
We have therefore reached for a 
compromise solution whereby par¬ 
ents may visit on three weekends: 
either Saturday, Sunday or Monday. 
We discourage visits during the first 


weekend but in a four-week stretch, 
there is still plenty of time left. 

If a parent cannot come on one of 
these days, we ask them to let us 
know which other day would be 
suitable, and they come when it is 
convenient. We ask them to bring a 
picnic lunch and we provide a little 
changing hut, as well as picnic tables 
at the beach, where they can be 
independent of the camp during 
meals and swims. This facility is 
somewhat taxed on the two busy 
Saturdays when most parents come, 
but the program is in no way 
changed on those days. 

During the visit a camper will 
show his parents around, introduce

NOUVELLES DU QUEBEC 
par Huguette L. Dagenais 

Recemment l’A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. te- 
nait un seminar a l’intention des 
directeurs de camp et de leurs princi- 
paux collaborateurs. 115 personnes 
ont participe aux assises de ce 
seminar et durant la fin de semaine 
ces personnes ont discute de poli- 
tiques de personnel ct des questions 
de financement dans les camps. Sans 
traduction simultanee, anglais et 
frangais ont echange en s’exprimant 
dans leur propre langue; des anima- 
teurs bilingues faisaient le lien. Un 
climat chaud ct amical regnait tout 
au long du “week-end”. Ce genre de 
seminar a certainement une valeur 
de recyclage et un certificat, accre- 
ditant les personnes qui ont suivi ce 
stage, devrait etre emis par le conseil 
provincial. 

Au cours de cette meme fin de 
semaine avait lieu l’assemblee an- 
nuelle. Au nouveau president; M. 
Robert Lazanik, meilleurs voeux de 
succes. A M. Lionel Perras, Presi¬ 
dent sortant et recipiendaire de 
l’insigne A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. Bravo et 
merci pour votre magnifique travail 
au sein de Y Association. 

Treize (13) personnes represen- 
taient le Quebe au Congres de 
l’A.C.C. a Halifax. 


Cont'd from Page 8 

As I write this I can not help but 
think of fellow staff members in our 
camps who have taken drugs. I am 
aware also of those who are dis¬ 
turbed with the present socio¬ 
political climate in the United States 
and Canada. However, I feel that 
their character and high moral in¬ 
tegrity are such that it would be 
inconsistent with our goals to ter¬ 
minate their presence in our camps. 

When a camp operates on prin¬ 
ciples of love and understanding it 
should never be necessary to impose 
on campers the personal life-styles 
(political, social, or religious) of 
individual staff members. We are 
guiding children with these basic 
moral ethics in order that he or she 
may develop these principles further 
during their own lives as they see fit. 

Physical appearance and super¬ 
ficial traits should not be allowed to 
influence one’s appreciation of a 
person’s potential as a human being. 

When we can see past all of this 
and begin to look into his or her 
mind, then and only then can we 
rightfully commence to appraise the 
person in terms of their value to one 
of our camps. We can learn from 
children here, for on the first day of 
camp a child discovers what his 


counsellor looks like and from the 
second day forward the child begins 
to recognize the counsellor as a 
fellow human being. 

I have looked into the minds of 
young working people, students, and 
camp personnel and have come 
away feeling tremendously confident 
in a youth culture filled with a pro¬ 
found moral concern for the future 
of our children and their society. 

It is my hope that we can further 
develop the trust and understanding 
of youth in the older generations, 
and the older generations in youth. 

Each of us in our own lives must 
help gain the respect of youth if we 
are to achieve human understanding 
and hence the continued existence 
of our camps in the interests of a 
better world. 

Let us have cause to nurture 
optimism!

Bryan Mitchell

OUTDOOR 

Editors Note : From the many 
recipes in the Cookbook entitled 
“Cookery for Kids, Kamp n Kicks” 
compiled by Helen E. Stewart, avail¬ 
able from Alvie Publications, 240 
Markland Drive, Apt. 510, Etobi¬ 
coke at $3.50 per copy. 

CAMPFIRE STEW 
2Vi lb. hamburg 

2 large onions 

1 tblsp. fat 

4 10 oz. cans soup— 

1 tomato, 3 vegetable 
Salt and pepper 

Make small balls of hamburg. Add 
seasoning. Fry with onions until 
onions are light brown and balls are 
well browned. Pour off excess fat, 
add soup and enough water to pre¬ 
vent sticking. Cover and cook slowly 
until meat balls are cooked through¬ 
out. 

TEXAS TOMMIES 
Slit a wiener lengthwise and insert 
a piece of cheese. Wrap a slice of 
bacon around the wiener and fasten 
with toothpicks. It can be cooked in 
a frying pan but it is better to cook 
it on a green stick. Can be eaten in 
a hotdog roll or a slice of bread. 

THE HOT DINNER PACKAGE 
Lay a bacon strip or two on a piece 
of foil. On this place a large ham¬ 
burg patty. Top with some finely 
sliced potatoes, onions, carrots, or 
other vegetables. Add salt, pepper 
and a pat of butter (if you wish). 
Fold this into a double packet. This 
can be done the night before and 
left overnight in refrigerator. Cook 
package over hot coals. 

Variations— 

—slice of ham, topped with sweet 
potato and apple slices 
—chicken leg or breast with bacon, 
slices and carrot slices 
—liver, bacon and onions 

ENERGY BARS 

Combine in a skillet over moderate 
heat about 2 cups of any one of a 
combination of ready-to-eat cereals 
— e.g. “Grapenuts”, and “Bran 
Flakes”; plus some raisins, nuts or 
coconut. The heating will crisp 
these ingredients. Remove from heat 
and stir in, until melted, about 1 
cup (6 oz. pkg.) of pieces of semi¬ 
sweet chocolate. When everything 
is stirred until well coated with 
chocolate, drop by spoonfuls onto 
waxed paper or foil and let stand 
until firm. (The mixture will be 


COOKERY 

very thick and hard to stir.) For use 
on trips, pat the mixture solidly into 
a muffin tin and turn out the cakes 
when they have cooled. Wrap in 
aluminum foil. If possible, make 
them in a double boiler, rather than 
in a skillet. Makes 16. 

POCKET STEW 
2 lb. hamburger meat 
8 large potatoes 
8 large carrots 
3-4 large onions 
Vi lb. butter 
10 ft. tin foil 

Salt and pepper 
(for each boy) 
l A lb. meat 
1 large potato 
1 large carrot 
Vi large onion 
Butter 

Tinfoil—1 foot 
Instructions for each boy: 

Make 1 large meat patty (flat—14" 
thick, 4" x 3"). Slice potatoes and 
carrots (slices should not be more 
than 14" thick). Dice or chop onion 
—rub butter on part of tinfoil 
which will be in contact with food. 
(Can put extra butter in also). 
Place food in layers— 

1. Meat in very centre. 

2. Either potatoes or carrots on the 
outside. 

Note: Shiny side of tinfoil should 
be inside. Entire stew, when folded, 
should be approx. 6" x 4" x 2 V 2 ". 
Note: Should be no more than 2 
layers of tinfoil around stew, and 
no less. Also, no holes in tinfoil. 
Cook in coals—10 minutes on each 
side. 


Lightning Fallacies 

Certain popular ideas about light¬ 
ning are not true, including: 

Lightning follows drafts. 

Electrical insulation will stop 
lightning. 

Under the bed or in a dark closet 
is the safest place in a thunder¬ 
storm. 

Lightning rods prevent lightning 
strokes. 

No lightning protection is effec¬ 
tive without a good ground. 

Balls or other ornaments on ele¬ 
vation rods of a lightning pro¬ 
tection system are essential to 
their proper functioning. 


SKILLET DINNER 

3 tblsp. shortening 

1 medium sized onion, sliced 
1 lb. lean ground beef 
!4 tsp. pepper 
1 can red kidney beans 
1 can kernel corn, drained 

1 tsp. garlic salt 

Cook onion in skillet in shortening 
until tender. Remove onion from 
skillet, leaving the hot fat. Break 
ground beef into small pieces and 
brown slowly. When meat is light 
brown, pour off the fat and add the 
onion, beans, corn, salt and pepper. 
Simmer in skillet about 10 minutes. 

S’MORES 

2 small squares sweetened chocolate 
2 marshmallows 

4 graham crackers 

Toast marshmallows over hot coals 
to a golden brown. Put square of 
chocolate on graham wafer. Cover 
with toasted marshmallow and add 
another graham cracker. Squeeze 
together and eat. 

BARBECUED SPICED BANANAS 
Peel bananas. Place each on a 
double thickness of foil. Brush with 
lemon juice. Sprinkle generously 
with brown sugar, dust with cin¬ 
namon or nutmeg, dot with mar¬ 
garine. Wrap the foil securely 
around the bananas, twisting ends. 
Cook on grill 7-9 minutes.

them to his counsellor, but after a

—Bruno Morawetz, PhD. 

CAMP BRIGADOON 

The Welcome Mat is always out 
at Brigadoon. While we ask parents 
not to visit campers for the first two 
weeks of camp, every day is, in real¬ 
ity, a possible visiting day; and it 
seems to work very well. Let me 
hasten to add, however, that ours is 
a camp small in numbers . . . thirty 
campers and twelve staff. We have 
always felt that if parents are visit¬ 
ing or holidaying in the area, or if 
father should be passing by on busi¬ 
ness or a fishing trip, they have a 
right to see their children. Widi 
our numbers, we can write such 
privileges into the regulations, where 
a camp of two hundred or more 
could not possibly cope with daily 
hordes of parents, friends, relatives, 
dogs, Siamese cats, budgies and 
white mice, not to mention numer¬ 
ous other small cherubs clinging to 
Mummy’s knees. 


Surprisingly, we find that our 
system, for us, does not get out of 
hand. Parents respect the two-week 
breaking-in period. Seldom do more 
than two or three, at most, visit si¬ 
multaneously, other than on the 
prescribed days. Our duties and 
work are such that either can be 
delegated or handled temporarily 
for the short time of the visit, which 
allows us ample time for the quiet 
talk (or consultation, if necessary), 
over coffee-and-a-bun, a visit with 
the children, a look at programme 
as it is, and a tour of buildings and 
facilities. We enjoy getting to know 
parents singly rather than in the 
busy group. 

Should we be out of camp, we 
leave instructions that visitors may 
see the camp and their campers at 
the end of the programme period, 
and wait for our return if this is 
convenient for them. 

The idea may not work for others, 
but we like it this way. 

—Eanswythe Flynn 

POWTER’S CAMP FOR BOYS 
St. Donat de Montcalm, Quebec 

Parents are allowed to visit 
Powter’s Camp for Boys every Sun¬ 


day except the first Sunday of each 
month. Visiting hours are from 
10:00 A.M. to 5:00 P.M. Parents 
are permitted to take their children 
out for lunch or may eat with them 
in various picnic areas on the camp 
property. 

Staff may have visitors up on 
Sunday but may only be with them 
in non-scheduled time. We do not 
provide meals or accommodation for 
staff visitors at the Counsellor level 
although permission is sometimes 
granted to members of the Senior 
Staff. 

—C. B. Powter 


FIRE HOSE 

If pressurized water is avail¬ 
able then sufficient garden 
hose with an adjustable spray 
and straight stream nozzle 
attached should be installed 
for additional protection. Re¬ 
member, a 2 Vi-gallon water 
extinguisher lasts about one 
minute but a garden hose will 
last until the well runs dry. 

Bryan Mitchell

Continued from Page 9 
all members of the camp. In order 
to facilitate the working of such a 
program there must be a strong sense 
of community in the camp. Each 
and every individual concerned must 
be focusing his energy in an effort to 
fulfill the camp philosophy. 

All sections of program may be 
treated in a similar manner. Arts 
and crafts should concentrate on 
creative design rather than simple 
picture making or assemblage of kits. 
Natural materials should be used as 
far as possible to bring about an 
appreciation of beauty in the exist¬ 
ing forms in nature. 

Music and dancing which play a 
very important part in camp life, can 
be expanded from note singing of 
old camp songs to include chanting, 
hand clapping, screaming and free¬ 
form dancing. A lesson can be 
learned from the satisfaction that 
the so called “primitive” savages 
obtain from their frenzied dancing 
around a flickering fire. These tribal 
rites depend solely on natural 
rhythms and movements of the 
human body to impart meaning. 

Swimming, canoeing and all 
other sections of the programming 
may be treated in a similar manner. 
The emphasis should not be placed 
on the camper’s ability to perform 
simply for testing purposes. Rather 


the approach used should impart a 
sense of usefulness to all skills 
learned. The fun and recreational 
possibilities in later years through 
application of skills should be 
stressed as well as a respect for and 
the proper care of the equipment 
concerned. As a result the camper 
will have not just a few dog-eared 
achievement cards to carry home but 
will be eager to continue with these 
activities at a later date. 

The use and acquisition of these 
learned skills takes a greater mean¬ 
ing when viewed in the wider per¬ 
spective of our society. There is an 
increasing amount of leisure time 
being made available to all members 
of our society. It is easy to under¬ 
stand the importance of wise use of 
this leisure time, not only for rea¬ 
sons of physical health but also for 
the all important aspect of mental 
health. 

It should be noted however that 
in order for this use of leisure time 
to be possible there must exist suit¬ 
able recreation areas. Once again 
this seems to revert back to the idea 
of conservation of natural areas and 
of the education of the public in this 
regard. 

The C.C.A. is probably one of the 
most efficient tools with which to 
convey this idea to the people of 
Canada. 


One of the visible effects of the 
fine work that our camps have been 
doing in the past is the increasing 
number of transient youths that ap¬ 
pear each summer on our roads. 
Here one can see the direct applica¬ 
tion of woodcraft and camping skills 
as more and more youth each year 
are hiking across the land with all 
their belongings in a single pack. If 
you happen across an encampment 
of such transients this summer stop 
by their fire under the stars and 
share with them the “joie de vivre” 
that they find in the freedom of 
open places. 

The question arises not so much 
whether or not youth are changing 
camps or camps changing youth but 
whether or not change is making 
youth camp. 


CHECK YOUR 
EQUIPMENT 

All camp cooking, refrigeration 
and heating equipment should 
be checked annually by a qual¬ 
ified serviceman. If propane 
from an outside storage tank is 
used it, too, should be installed 
by a qualified mechanic in a 
location on solid ground away 
from windows and well se¬ 
cured. Bryan Mitchell

IT'S FOR THE BIRDS! 

by Eanswythe Flynn 


Certain plants and shrubs 
attract particular types of birds 
and animals to your camp 
area. Try planting with their 
living quarters and feeding 
stations in mind. 


Ours was never a particularly 
large garden at home. Vegetables 
grew in their proper place. But 
there were flowers, great clumps of 
the English Garden variety, among 
them the Nicotine Plant, now com¬ 
mon to most parts of Canada. This 
very plant recalls a cherished child¬ 
hood memory of hummingbirds 
darting in and out of the fragrant 
blossoms all summer long. One 
could sit close by for any length of 
time watching their delicate iri¬ 
descent wings, noting the variations 
in colour. All this, in the heart of 
the city. 

Not often is this particular plant 
seen in any abundance now, and 
we wonder why. Surely it would 
grow and blossom, with care, in a 
north-country garden if the plants 
were started in the city. This is only 
one of many flowers on the cultiva¬ 
tion list for a special garden corner 
at camp. How else to lure these tiny 
wing-ed jewels to an observation 
post for campers to create instant 
programme? 

With a little study plus the help 
of student ecologists and Garden 
Club enthusiasts, the whole camp 
area can become a sanctuary for all 
kinds of wildlife, particularly birds. 
A good habitat is already established 
as a basis in most camps, with much 


of the natural flora acting as a haven 
for feeding and production. Any 
additional planting can become a 
year-to-year project. 

It would be impossible to list here 
the infinite variety of plants, shrubs 
and trees one might consider. An 
excellent book, entertainingly writ¬ 
ten, containing lists, tables and 
charts, is John K. Terres’, “Song¬ 
birds In Your Garden” (Fitzhenry 
and Whiteside, Toronto. $8.75). 
Information is also available through 
local conservation Authorities, and 
Departments of Lands and Forests. 

BUCKWHEAT seeds are noted 
for high fat content; favoured feed¬ 
ing for Hungarian partridge and 
other birds. 

CORN attracts Ring - necked 
Pheasant, smaller birds and our 
ever-present friends, the Racoons. 

HIGHBUSH CRANBERRY, a 
favourite of Ruffed Grouse and 
Woodpeckers. 

SUMAC fruit endure the winter 
to feed Kinglets, Chickadees, Nut¬ 
hatches, Winter Finches, Grossbeaks 
and Cardinals. 

CEDARS really do attract Cedar 
Waxwings, literally by the hundred. 
The birds are “colour co-ordinated” 
with the trees, but if one stands still 
to watch them in a cedar grove, 
they become very brave and perch 
near enough to be seen and studied. 
Vain creatures, indeed! 

WILD CHERRY is a banquet for 
Robins, Catbirds, Thrushes and 
Thrashers. 

PINE, BIRCH, DOGWOOD — 
all are very important to all song¬ 
birds. 


ELM in its healthy state is the 
natural home of the Oriole. Finches 
and Grosbeaks eat its buds and 
seeds. 

BOX ELDER is important to 
Evening Grosbeaks. 

MULBERRY has a great attrac¬ 
tion to all birds during the summer 
as well as during migration. Plant it 
away from a paved area, as the 
berries “dribble” a deep purple. 

PINCHERRY has been known to 
attract as many as twenty-five kinds 
of birds at one time. 

For the flower garden: Asters, 
Cornflowers, Larkspur, Cosmos, 
Gaillardias, Calendula, Bell-flowers, 
Chrysanthemums, Columbines, For¬ 
get-me-nots, Marigolds, Sunflowers, 
Verbena, Zinnia, Poppies, Phlox. 
You will be blessed with such lovely 
creatures as Quail, Buntings, Juncos, 
Larks, White-throated Sparrows, 
Song Sparrows, Towhees, Black¬ 
birds, during spring, summer and 
fall. Save all the seeds from any of 
these- flowers and put them out for 
winter feeding. 

Perhaps most important of all the 
seeds is that of the Sunflower. Toss 
them on lawn or garden at any time 
of the year. Birds enjoy them and 
will, at the same time, keep your 
area free of destructive insects. 

Doubtless there are many natur¬ 
alists among our members who can 
add to this list, as well as those who 
have already experimented with 
such a project. The Editorial Com- 
mitee would like to hear of these 
efforts and relay further information 
through articles from other writers.
