Continued from Page 24 
You must not pour water on to 
this grease fire because you are liable 
to be burned by either the hot steam, 
the spitting, burning grease or bodi. 
You must not attempt to run outside 
with a burning pan of grease. The 
flames will burn your hands, causing 
you to drop the pan, and the fire 
will spread in size. 

Water is an excellent extinguisher 
for fires in wood, paper, grass, mat¬ 
tresses, furniture, etc. It may be 
poured on to the fire from a pail, or 
sprayed on to the fire from a garden 
hose. It may be pumped from a 2 V 2 - 
gallon or 5-gallon pump tank or it 
may be discharged on to a fire from 
a soda-acid or pressurized water 
extinguisher. Know your fire ex¬ 
tinguisher, know where it is kept, 
know how it operates (read the di¬ 
rections on the label), know what 
type of fire it can be used on. 
CLASSIFICATION OF FIRES 
Class “A”—Ordinary combustibles 
—wood, paper, cloth, etc. 

Class “B”—Flammable liquids— 
gasoline, oils, paints, etc. 

Class “C”—Energized electrical— 
motors, radios, T.V.’s, wires, etc. 
Class “A” fires—use a water pump 
tank, soda-acid, foam, pressurized 
water extinguisher or a garden 
hose. 

Class “B” fires—use a C0 2 (carbon 
dioxide), dry chemical (baking 
soda) or a foam extinguisher. 
NEVER use water. 

Class “C” fires—use a C0 2 or dry 
chemical. NEVER use water. 
Buildings on campgrounds should 
have only extinguishers that are 
“approved” by a recognized testing 
agency. One of the following names 
or insignia should appear on the 
extinguisher label. 

1. Underwriters Laboratories In¬ 
corporated, or U.L.C. approved. 

2. Underwriters’ Laboratories of 
Canada, or U.L.C. approved. 

3. Factory Mutual or FM ap¬ 
proved. 

4. British Fire Office or BFO 
approved. 

These extinguishers may cost a 
little more but they are designed to 
extinguish a given amount of fire. 
The cheaper aerosol or beer can type 
extinguishers that are sold in hard¬ 
ware stores, tire stores, are not ap¬ 
proved and should not be relied 
upon. 

The most common types found in 
camps are the 2Vi -gallon pump type 
water extinguisher and the 5 lb dry 
chemical for kitchen and electrical 
fires. 

The owner of a camp or the Chief 
Ranger should have an Emergency 


Telephone Number List on display 
near all telephones in the camp 
area. This list should contain the 
numbers to reach the nearest mu¬ 
nicipal fire department and/or the 
nearest Lands and Forests fire¬ 
fighters. The nearest municipal, 
provincial or R.C.M.P. police de¬ 
partment should be included as well 
as the number of the nearest doctor 
or hospital Red Cross branch or St. 
John first aid station. The list should 
also show the number of the ambu¬ 
lance and the nearest oxygen resus- 
citator. 

A camp should always have a 
large first aid kit and personnel 
trained in administering first aid. 
Many a burn victim has been forced 
to suffer additional pain because an 
untrained person smeared butter or 
salve on to a third degree burn and 
this had to be removed at the hos¬ 
pital before proper treatment could 
be commenced. 

In small minor burns one of the 
easiest treatments is to submerge the 
burned area in a dish of ice water. 
In large area burns wrap the victim 
in a sterile dressing or a clean bed 
sheet and rush him to the nearest 
doctor or hospital. 

If a camper’s clothing catches 
fire, trip him if he is running, roll 
him on the ground, smother him 
with a coat, blanket or even your 
own body to extinguish the flames. 
Your quick action may save his life. 
Once the fire is out treat for burns 
and shock. 

Associated with camping is the 
fire hazard of boating. With the use 
of both inboard and outboard motors 
we are again faced with the fire and 
vapour hazards of gasoline. 

The outboard motor should never 
be filled when it is hot. If portable 
auxiliary gas tanks are used they 
should be removed from the boat 
during filling operations. Before fill¬ 
ing motors or gas tanks make sure 
no-one is smoking in or near the 
boat. Do not overload the tanks but 
allow for expansion. Mop up any 
spillage immediately. 

The inboard motors may present 
an even greater danger during filling 
and starting operations. In some of 
the older boats the fill pipes do not 
extend to the bottom of the gas tank. 
The vent pipes may discharge into 
the hull instead of to the outside. 
During the filling operations the 
nozzle must make metal-to-metal 
contact with the fill pipe to prevent 
static electricity from causing an 
explosion. After filling mop up spill¬ 
age and secure fill cap tightly. 

Before starting an inboard motor 
always remember to open all ports, 


28 



doors, etc. and ventilate for five 
minutes. During the start-up period 
make sure your extinguisher is 
handy and that no-one is smoking. 

Just as a life preserver may save 
your life if your boat capsizes, these 
life safety rules may save your life 
during re-fuelling and starting 
operations. 

RULES FOR FIRE-SAFE 
CAMPING 

If campers would all take a little 
bit of their time to learn the Dos 
and Don’ts of Fire Safe Camping, 
we would not have our annual toll 
of injuries and death! Canada would 
not have as many forest fires and 
these forests and lakes would remain 
with us for other campers to enjoy 
in the years to come. 

1. DO obtain a fire permit from a 
fire ranger or the Department 
of Lands and Forests. 

2. DO use the camp’s fireplaces or 
fire pits. 

3. In wilderness camping DO 
clear an area four to ten feet in 
diameter for your fire. 

4. DON’T build a fire under over¬ 
hanging branches. 

5. DO keep your fire small, never 
leave it unattended, and put it 
"dead out’’. 

6. DON’T use flammable liquids 
to start a fire. 

7. DO keep flammable liquids in 
clearly marked metal containers 
and away from children. 

8. DO fill heating, lighting and 
cooking equipment when die 
appliance is cool. 

9. DON’T fill or light appliances 
inside a tent or camp building. 

10. DO keep an extinguisher handy 
and know how it works. 

11. DO know how to extinguish 
brush or grass fires with a 
shovel, wet sack or broom. 

12. DO learn first aid and carry a 
well-stocked first aid kit. 

13. DON’T smoke while fuelling 


FLAMMABLE LIQUIDS 
Flammable liquids such as 
gasoline, kerosene, alcohol, etc. 
should be kept in approved 
metal containers and stored in 
a locked shed away from other 
camp buildings. This building 
should be placarded to alert 
others to the danger of its con¬ 
tents. This same building can 
be used to house marine lubri¬ 
cants and engine oils, as none 
of these is susceptible to spon¬ 
taneous ignition. 

Bryan Mitchell 


your boat motor or auxiliary gas 
tanks. 

14. DO become a fire-safe camper. 

A FOOT TRAIL ACROSS 
CANADA 

by Ann Prewitt 
Editor, Canadian Camping 

Mr. L. Doug Campbell of the 
Chinook Trail Association, Calgary, 
Alberta, originated the idea of a 
cross-Canada hiking trail. The ob¬ 
jectives of the trail are: 

To preserve places of natural and 
historical value. 

To promote healthy outdoor ac¬ 
tivities. 

To foster interest in the natural 
environment. 

To develop a national and nat¬ 
ural resource. 

To strengthen national ties. 

To provide places to enjoy leisure 
amid the natural scene. 

As the official representative of 
the Canadian Camping Association 
(appointed by the Board in Halifax) 
I attended the organizational meet¬ 
ing held at the Toronto YMCA on 
April 29th, 1971. 

Other organizations represented 
at the meeting included the Boy 
Scouts, Girl Guides, YM-YWCA’s, 
National and Provincial Parks As¬ 
sociations, Dept, of National Health 
and Welfare, Waskahegan Trail 
Assoc. (Alberta), Bruce Trail 
Assoc., Canadian Audubon Society, 
The Federation of Ontario Natur¬ 
alists, and other interested individ¬ 
uals. 

Copies of Canadian Camping 
Association’s Centenary Journal 
“JOURNAL” have since been sent 
to the organizational leaders of the 
foot trail. 

Anyone who is interested in as¬ 
sisting with this project should write 
to Mr. W. H. Carrick, 387 Kort- 
right Road, Guelph, Ontario. Mr. 
Carrick (of the Canadian Audubon 
Society) has volunteered to collect 
maps of all existing trails that may 
be sent to him and the names of 
those who are interested. Please let 
Mr. Carrick know that you are a 
member of the Canadian Camping 
Association and indicate if you sup¬ 
port the idea of a Cross-Canada 
Trail or if you have time to give 
more organizational and leadership 
help in your Province or locality. 
The Representative of the Depart¬ 
ment of National Health and Wel¬ 
fare indicated that funds would be 
available to bring representatives to 
an organizational meeting in the fall 
if we find there is sufficient interest 
across Canada to establish a trail.

ARTS AND CRAFTS 
FIRE HAZARD 

There are two areas where we 
may find spontaneous ignition 
occurring. The first is from the 
rags used by the painters or 
maintenance personnel who 
clean their hands with turpen¬ 
tine-soaked rags, and the same 
is true if children are using 
these materials to finish the 
articles made during their Arts 
and Crafts lessons. These oily 
rags must either be burned (by 
an adult) or put into a metal 
container with a tightly-closed 
lid. Contrary to old wives' 
tales, other greases such as 
those used in cooking, etc., are 
not generally susceptible to 
spontaneous ignition. 

Bryan Mitchell 


Personal Conduct in Thunderstorms 

(a) Do not go out of doors or re¬ 
main out during thunderstorms 
unless it is necessary. Stay inside of 
a building where it is dry, preferably 
away from fireplaces, stoves, and 
other metal objects. 

(b) If there is any choice of shelter, 
choose in the following order: 

(1) Large metal or metal-framed 
buildings. 

(2) Dwellings or other buildings 
which are protected against 
lightning. 

(3) Large unprotected buildings. 

(4) Small unprotected buildings. 

(c) If remaining out of doors is 
unavoidable, keep away from: 

(1) Small sheds and shelters if in 
an exposed location. 

(2) Isolated trees. 

(3) Wire fences.

THE SIGN

Dear Mommy & Daddy, 


You told me to drop you a line, so. 


guess 


you don't think that's very funny, but I did and 
so did my new friend Suzie. She's my friend now, 
but she wasn't yesterday because she hurt me. 

It was all her fault; when Miss Smith was showing 
us all how to put a tent up, Suzie was supposed 
to hammer in the wedge for the loop for the tent ropes and the hammer 
hit me in the chin. Dumb Suzie! 



Miss Smith said "Calm Down" just like you say. Mommy. And then we went to the 
Dentist in town. My tooth was broken and had to come out. I can't eat any of the peanut 
brittle you sent; it was yellow anyway. 

Miss Smith says "Don't forget to tell your parents that the camp has Camp-Guard 
and Camp-Guard will take care of the Dentist's bills." 

So that's what I'm doing at camp. I don't like Suzie again because my mouth is still 
sore. 

Love Janie
